utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, while we are waiting for the witness, good afternoon, shall we hear your decision about the question that we asked yesterday about a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, as I said yesterday, this Trial Chamber is deliberating the motions you filed just now. And this morning, we received the response from the Prosecution. We haven't had enough time to consider it yet. I believe that after the last witness, we'll make the proper decisions at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Would you please sit down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if we could go to private session just for a couple more minutes, hopefully while finish my questions in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know who was the commander of the Convicts Battalion in 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Ivan Andabak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever present at the headquarters of the Convicts Battalion in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had our defence office, which was near the Convicts Battalion office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again, sir, because of the time, I'm going to ask you to please listen to my question and be very specific. Were you ever in the headquarters offices of the Convicts Battalion in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I was in the headquarters of the Convicts Battalion in Siroki Brijeg, visiting it together with my defence office.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many times were you in this headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not often. I cannot give you the exact number of times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Twice, three times? When you say not very often, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would guess so. Not often, two, three, four times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to be very clear, sir. I'm not asking, and in the interests of time I'm not going to try to pull out the photograph, I'm not talking about your being in the building, the house that is in the front part, if you will, of the tobacco factory. I'm not asking you how many times you were in that building. I'm asking you how many times you were in the headquarters, the actual offices dedicated to the Convicts Battalion. Now, do you understand that and is your answer then the same or different?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not understand where is the headquarters, where is the command of the Convicts Battalion, according to you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you know where the Convicts Battalion headquarters was, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The office of the Convicts Battalion, I pointed at it yesterday. If you give me the photograph again, I will show you exactly where that office was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have established we both know where it was, sir. With that additional foundation, were you in that office ever in 1993, that office, not the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't my business to visit either the headquarters or anything, because we had the Defence office, which communicated with those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any meetings or briefings of the commanders of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never present, nor did it fall within my terms of reference, nor was that my duty. Because I -- I'm not familiar with the military affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it from your answer, sir, that the answer would be the same to the question: Were you ever present or involved in any meetings at the HVO Main Staff in Mostar? Did you ever attend any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my duty. It was done by people who were responsible for that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you weren't --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a military -- the military structure of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So are you telling the Judges, sir, that as to military matters of the HVO, you do not have any knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My part of the job, I repeat again, [redacted] [redacted] means that I never had any say in the matters relative to the other component. Those were military matters. And I do not know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said there was a special purpose unit that was part of the Convicts Battalion, if I heard you correctly. What was the name of that unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Convicts Battalion was the unit for special purposes, i.e. the unit for interventions, and I don't know, I'm not familiar with the structure of the units of the Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So when you told us yesterday, and it may have been my -- I didn't hear you correctly, sir, when you talked about a special purpose unit, you were talking about the entire Convicts Battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of the civilian police or what might be called the MUP in Siroki Brijeg in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The MUP in Siroki Brijeg, and in all the neighbouring towns, were part of the structure of the MUP of Herzegovina in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I understand that, sir, but there must have been a local, who was the local leader or commander or officer in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I told you yesterday, when I read to you the names of all the members of the HVO, and I also read the name of the gentleman who was in charge of that. His name was Danko Bilinovac. I know his name because we cooperated. And again because he is a -- my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you tell us who was in charge of the military police in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I couldn't tell you because the military police was not under the jurisdiction of the civilian authorities in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was the head of the Home Guard in Siroki Brijeg in 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had, as far as I can remember, several battalions. I think that there were three battalions, and their commanders changed quite often. As far as I can remember, after Mr. Cavar, Mr. Cavar was succeeded by Mr. Sasko. Unfortunately he is no longer amongst the living, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right, now, sir, can you tell us, in terms of any Muslim men who were prisoners, detainees or prisoners in Siroki Brijeg in 1993, who or what organisation in Siroki Brijeg had custody and care of those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: These detainees were brought by the military police, since they didn't have enough room to accommodate these people, they asked the Defence Department whether they could help them with the accommodation of those people, and then they accommodated them in the premises of the civilian police. And that is -- they gave them the custody over these detainees. Since the civilian police took over the care of these detainees, I don't know why, for what reason, I suppose they were either there for interrogation or they were waiting for exchanged. We as the civilian part of the HVO were -- had a duty to look after these people, and this is what we did. I was informed --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... going to go on because again our time is limited.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can the usher please assist me in showing the witness Exhibits P665 and 697?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to direct your attention first of all to 665 and of course you can look at the Croatian language version. Sir, this is a communication dated the 10th of November, 1993, from Bruno Stojic, the Minister of Defence, titled or addressed to, to the commander of the Convicts Battalion, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, personally. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps the usher can assist you. 665. That's it. Sir, is it not addressed in the right side of the page in the Croatian version, is it not addressed to, does it not say, "To the commander of the Convicts Battalion, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, personally"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at Exhibit P697? Sir, this is a communication dated the 26th of November, 1993, from a Colonel Marijan Biskic who was the head of the security sector of the HVO Main Staff, and does he not also address this to, "HVO, Convicts Battalion, personally, commander, Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can see it, yes, that is correct, but I don't know what -- how could I comment this, as the President of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you telling these Judges -- are you telling the Judges under oath that the Minister of Defence, Bruno Stojic, and the head of the HVO Main Staff for the security sector, Marijan Biskic they didn't know who the commander of the Convicts Battalion was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They should know who the commander of the Convicts Battalion was. That is why I'm surprised to find the name of Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'd agree with me, sir, wouldn't you and you just said this it a few minutes ago, the Minister of Defence and the head of the security sector know more about HVO military matters than you do, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They must do, because I simply don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown Exhibit P578?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a communication from, again, Bruno Stojic dated the 26th of August, 1993, and under the name that are listed, I'll come back to the names in a moment, Mr. Stojic says, "All the above named persons employed in the court and the prosecutor's Office, which will be unable to carry on their duties without them." Now in the Croatian version, do you see, to the left of those names, there is a bracket or whatever -- bracket or parenthesis, on the left side of those list of seven names with a handwritten notation, "These men, Tuta"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, perhaps you can assist the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see the handwritten part, sir, in the Croatian version to the left of the seven names, a word that appears to be "Tuta" with two words that appear to be above that? Do you see that, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but anybody could write "Tuta."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, look down at the bottom left-hand part of the page. Does it not say in Croatian, "Colonel Cavar, please urgently exempt these men so that the civilian authorities can function. Tuta"? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that but I don't know whether this is Mr. Tuta's signature.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen his signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could have been signed by anybody.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen Mr. Tuta's signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even if I'd seen it, I did see it, but I have, in the meantime, forgotten how Mr. Tuta signs his name. This was a long time ago so it's very difficult for me to tell by just looking at this who this is. It could have been anybody from any unit or from anywhere. Anybody could have signed Tuta's name. It happened very often. And if you will allow me just a second, Mr. Prosecutor, I would like to tell you that, because of a number of instances of abuse, because of the things that were happening, we had to restore order because people abused the situation which was not normal. Everybody wanted to take the opportunity of gaining something for themselves. And very often it would happen that somebody would sign a document on behalf of somebody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. I appreciate -- you can't say whether it's Tuta's signature or not, all right? So because of the time we will go on. Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I kept quiet. I did not want to put any objections so far. Can I just draw your attention to the Croatian original? I don't know whether you have it in front of you. All my objections so far, when a minister writes to anybody, I doubt that he would send a piece of document without a stamp. A lot of things were written, added by hand, without any official -- excuse me, I'm here raising an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, you could raise the objection but you could not indicate any answer to this question. And if you have some objections, you have the full opportunity to do it when this document is tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, on the original, there is no signature. All it says, all we can see, is TU. And again, in the English translation, it gives the full name. So things have to be represented correctly. That's all I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, at my hand, I don't have those documents at this moment. I don't know the status of this document. But I was reminded by Madam Registrar that it has been admitted already into the evidence. So I think this matter is over. You may proceed, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not sure if I heard you correctly yesterday in connection with Mr. Martin Garrod, Sir Martin Garrod or not. Are you telling the Judges that there was never a meeting involving you, Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Garrod? Are you saying that there absolutely was never a meeting or are you telling the Chamber that you just don't remember one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Naletilic, Tuta, and Mr. Martin Garrod came to my place in Siroki Brijeg very often, and I will allow for the possibility that they did meet in Siroki Brijeg, but those were private visits which -- in which they talked about private matters, which are not binding. So I do not exclude the possibility --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So we agree that it's very possible or likely that, as you said, Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Garrod met in Siroki Brijeg, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a possibility, but they -- they were never together in a -- in my house, but somewhere else, they may have met, I don't exclude that possibility but I can't assert anything about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, you just said, I don't want to get bogged down by this too much but you just said a moment ago in line 23, you said, "Mr. Naletilic, Tuta, and Mr. Martin Garrod came to my place in Siroki Brijeg very often." Now, which is it? Did they come to your house or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did come to my house, but not together. Again, I repeat, there is a possibility that they saw each other when they were at my house, but never when I was there, because I wasn't there all the time. Mr. Garrod was my friend and he could come to my house any time of the day or night. Mr. Mladen Naletilic also is my friend. He did not have to announce his visit when he decided to visit me on a private matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, when you talk about having a private conversation, and a private conversation not being binding, are you telling us that it matters to you what you say, whether you think you're having a private conversation or some other kind of conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would always draw a line between a friendly chat and an official position of these same people when they talk about official things in the official part of that same conversation. I would draw a line between the two. Mr. Martin Garrod is a very nice, elderly gentleman, and he came -- we all liked him because he would very often offer his advice, his experience, in order to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to move on because time is limited?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor has already overstepped his ten minutes but I did not want to react, so he is -- has gone longer than my direct examination, and I think that it was agreed a long time ago that cross should not -- the time for the cross should not exceed the time for the direct examination. And I have two other witnesses that I would like to finish today. The weekend is coming, and I have another gentleman who has some health problems. We have two more witnesses today, don't we?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I quite understand that. And the -- I believe that the Prosecution is approaching to its end of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I would appreciate some more time with this witness. [redacted] . And the Chamber knows who he is, and he is claimed to be a very close friend of the accused and I would appreciate a few more minutes to ask him some questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in terms of the conversations that you have, in terms of your telling the truth, does it matter to you whether you're in a private conversation or some other type of conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you, Mr. Prosecutor, to repeat this question. I didn't quite understand it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, do you tell the truth whether you're in a private conversation or public conversation? Or does your truth telling depend on the nature of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, it depends on who I'm talking to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, sir, did you tell the truth to Martin Garrod or were you lying to Martin Garrod when you had conversations with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would never lie to Sir Garrod because there is no need to lie to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that a number of the Muslim refugees that came to Siroki Brijeg were later put on buses and taken to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, since Siroki Brijeg had a limited accommodation capacity, and a large number of refugees who were passing through Siroki Brijeg were taken by buses. I think to Croatia. I can't tell you exactly where in Croatia but I think it was somewhere in the southern part of Croatia, somewhere around Makarska.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these were Muslim refugees, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that they were Muslim refugees, and not only Muslims, there were also Croatian refugees there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, why weren't the Muslims allowed to go back to the parts of Bosnia that were controlled by the Muslim armed forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the foundation for this allegation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's a natural question, because those Muslims were bussed to Croatia so the next question will be the one the Prosecutor is asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is just an allegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He admitted, he stated it, Your Honour. He answered the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it all depends on how the witness is going to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Why weren't the Muslims allowed to go back to the parts of Bosnia under the Muslim armed forces control?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I don't know how familiar you are with the location of Siroki Brijeg. Siroki Brijeg is away from any roads that go to Bosnia. If you go through Siroki Brijeg, you end up in Croatia. And the people who sent these people to Siroki Brijeg, I believe that it is logical that they meant Croatia to be their final destination because Siroki Brijeg is on the way to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you're just assuming, you're now assuming that the Muslims, who for whatever reason appeared in Siroki Brijeg as refugees, you assume that they wanted to go on to Croatia. And that's why they were put on buses and take to Croatia. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Prosecutor does not have any foundation. He does not have any evidence. These are his speculations. He doesn't know whether the refugees wanted to go through Croatia or not, whether they wanted to go back to the area controlled by the BH Army. He doesn't know that. He just speculates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I don't think it's speculation in this instance. I think it's a natural question to ask this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where is the evidence for this allegations about where they wanted to go? Has he shown us any piece of evidence, any piece of document, showing us that the refugees did not end up where they wanted to end up? He can not assume where the refugees wanted to go or end up at. This was the wartime. I apologise, Your Honours, but these are nothing but speculations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think during the wartime, everybody wants to go back to his home town or to a safer place. We'll hear what the witness is going to tell us. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, he already -- the witness answered the question and it was the witness, not the Prosecutor who assumed, he said, "well, I assume they wanted to go to Croatia." And I believe the transcript will show that. And I simply followed up on that statement but I'm finished that line of questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like the usher to show you Exhibit D1/345. I'm trying, Mr. President, to move as quickly as I can. Sir, this decision makes reference to a decree on the rights and commitments of citizens temporarily employed abroad. Now, decree. Is that something that was like a law that was decided by the government of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision was passed by the HVO of Siroki Brijeg, and it was only binding on -- for the citizens of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but in the decision itself, it refers to a decree that apparently was published in the Narodni List, the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community Herceg-Bosna and the decree itself, is that something to your understanding that had the force of law as something enacted by the government of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can read it, Your Honours, it says, "Pursuant to Article 4 of the statutory decision of the municipal executive authority and the municipal administration, and this was adopted in January, 1992. That is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't know it would be that difficult a question for the witness, and I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm really worried now because I see that the Prosecutor has no intention, nor did he reorganise his questions, but he knew how much time he had at his disposal. This has been going on for 1 hour 15 minutes I need to begin with a third witness and I can not leave him like that. This is not nice. You interrupted me in my cross-examination if it was longer than allowed. The Prosecutor had time to prepare himself since yesterday. And ask concise questions but he has no intention of bringing to a close his cross-examination, and I think that the same rules that apply to me should apply to the Prosecutor in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, you have to wind up your cross-examination as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. I object to characterisations about my intentions because I'm sure that Mr. Krsnik has no idea about my intentions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Usher can you please show the witness Exhibit number P929? Mr. President, after this document, I will seek to put -- I will -- I have four other documents but I will seek to put a series of shorter questions to the witness and try not to use the documents and I'll to finish as soon as possible. P929. It should have been in the bundle that was put out yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, isn't it true that during 1993, there were -- the Croatian Army, and by that I mean the Republic of Croatia army, what's sometimes called the HV, and the MUP of the Republic of Croatia was present in Siroki Brijeg? And I direct your attention, sir, if it will assist you to point 6 of Exhibit P929. It says --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw this document before. Do I have time to read it?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only if the Chamber will allow it, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what it is about. I do not know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, the Prosecutor was asking you a question, that is whether the HV army were present in the Siroki Brijeg? And he also draw your attention to the paragraph 6 of that document. You could read that paragraph and answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I claim under full responsibility, Your Honours, that the Croatian Army was never in the territory of Siroki Brijeg. I do not know what this is about. I've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just for the record because we have to move on. I'm showing you this exhibit to give you a chance to respond to it and I put it to you that in this report to Mr. Minister, prepared by you and Mr. Saskor who you named earlier in your testimony as one of the local Home Guard commanders that you reported currently Siroki Brijeg has more than 6.000 armed soldiers including the Croatian Army and the MUP of the Republic of Croatia. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, where is this leading to? One can see with the naked eye that this was never signed so how can the Prosecutor allege that this is signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I didn't say it was signed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, this is a document showed by the Prosecutor, and this document has some basis because the names were put at the end of the document. So I think it's legitimate for the Prosecution to ask the question along this line. And your witness has the full right to answer that question, which will help us to understand the situation. There is no need for intervention on your part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the witness has said it twice that this was the first time that he's seen this document and they want him to react and then it is alleged that he signed it. And it is quite clear that he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have noticed that. We'll hear what the witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, under full responsibility, I say that before you, that the civilian authority has never asked anything, the civilian authority had never any applications or anything to submit to the military authority if we, the civilian authority, had some requests, then it was done by us, the civilian authority. The civilian authority and the military authority did not function together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with -- isn't -- excuse me. Isn't it true, sir, that the members of the Convicts Battalion Siroki Brijeg were notorious law breakers in the community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Laws were violated all over. It wasn't only a specific feature of the Convicts Battalion. There were individual incidents on all sides. And that includes the Convicts Battalion. But it wasn't a rule that applied to the Convicts Battalion alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember Miroslav Kolobara, Drazenko Farac, being charged with attempted murder on the 17th of November, 1993, in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the individuals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know the individual under that name, that person does not come from Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember Dalibor Kozul, Krsto Vukoje and Vinko Topic, all soldiers of the Convicts Battalion, being charged with rape on the 8th of November, 1993, in Siroki Brijeg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, certainly, you remember the incident, do not you, sir? Was rape that -- so common no November, 1993, in Siroki Brijeg, that you wouldn't remember a woman being raped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never heard of any rape in Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you told us -- during, you told us during your direct examination that you knew virtually everything that happened in Siroki Brijeg. You even knew if anyone carried out forced labour or not. You told us that could never have happened, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forced labour or rather people who came to Siroki Brijeg, they became part of Siroki Brijeg, and I had to take care of those people. Individual rapes? They were not --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, wasn't this woman part of Siroki Brijeg and wouldn't this be a terrible crime that you don't seem to know about? And yet you claim to know about everything else. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a horrible crime, I think, but believe me, Your Honours, that I never heard about that happening in the territory of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't have time, as the Chamber knows, but I refer just so the Chamber knows, I base this question on Exhibit P680 which is a report by the military police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is my final questions, Mr. President and I appreciate the Court's patience.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Isn't it true, sir, that there are many things that Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, was involved in that you simply don't know one way or the other, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please phrase it in a clearer way?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll give you more specifics, sir. You really don't have any knowledge of anything that Mr. Naletilic might have done, for instance at the Heliodrom or in the city of Mostar, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have any knowledge whether Mr. Mladen Naletilic was ever at the Heliodrom or in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you don't have any knowledge of anything that Mr. Naletilic did or might have done in Sovici Doljani in April of 1993, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean -- you mean the appeal of 1993? [redacted], [redacted], as you can see from the documents I got there on the 9th of July, 1993, and about that, I have no knowledge whether Mr. Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, or anyone else from the Convicts Battalion was in Sovici, that is I don't know what other place was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I cannot even -- I wanted to because I have to finish two witnesses. I wanted to be known that for an hour and 35 minutes, was the duration of the cross-examination, and the direct examination lasted -- took 45 minutes. I now simply have no more time to even ask anything in my redirect, nor do I want to ask him anything. I want to move on to other witnesses because we can not keep them for another week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, I don't think it's realistic to finish two witnesses today, today. I think at least one witness will have to be dealt with next week. We will try our best to finish one more witness today, but I'm not quite sure whether we could finish with two. I quite agree with you that the cross-examination took longer time than yours, which is not proper and it should be not allowed to happen again, but if you want to re-examine this witness, you ever the full rights to do so. We will break until the second session this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, very briefly, now, I won't have any additional questions because I prepared my witnesses for half hours, and I also modified my questions so that my direct examination of both these two witnesses would not take longer than 45 minutes and I'm quite sure that we can do it today. I shall be asking only specific questions and will seek their specific answers because they are witnesses to facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But it's time for a break. We'll break first. Yes. We'll resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it necessary to address you, when I left the courtroom after the break I do not think I behaved correctly towards you, and there is no reason for that. I'm a professional, and if I offended you in any way, please forgive me. I apologise and I promise it will never happen again. I believe I interrupted you, Mr. President, as you were speaking, and please receive my apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, your apology is accepted. And I just want to emphasise that whenever a Judge is speaking, there should be no interruptions at all. You may sit down, please. Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just a moment, before the witness comes back, I'd like to object on behalf of my Defence on the manner in which documents are presented during the cross-examination. I believe that it was in violation of the decisions taken by the Chamber earlier, on various occasions Mr. President, you said this was a document which has not been authorised, which has not been authenticated, that is a document maybe shown the witness and if the witness says that the -- he does not know the document, to then stop using this document, that such a document may not be used again. That is at least how I understood the position of the Chamber regarding the presentation of these documents. Secondly, a rule which we take to be the Chamber's position is that a document should not be read because it was said that the documents speak for themselves. Today, we were in a situation to see that some documents are produced here in a manner which runs counter to these decisions, and we are in faced with a situation that a document which will not be tendered into evidence or cannot be admitted because it has not been authenticated, that it is not tendered, but the contents of that document are nevertheless presented, that is the Prosecutor reads such documents. And I do not think that that is really all right. Because in this way, this document becomes evidence, because the transcript is evidence. And now, if a document, perhaps is not tendered into evidence, and its contents nevertheless may become part of the transcript because the Prosecutor has read the document, then we once again have something that we are objecting to and which is contrary to the decisions of the Chamber. I would like to hear the opinion of the Chamber on this matter because I think this is a problem which perhaps will keep cropping up again, and it happened yesterday when our learned friends pointed out that when certain documents are offered to be read, there will -- that they would not be tendered but would -- but the Chamber would nevertheless be acquainted with them, and I'd like that an end be put to that, to such a practice, because we object to it and during the Prosecutor's case, we were not allowed to use the same method. There were times when we tried to present certain documents in this manner. This was prevented and these decisions that I'm now referring to were made on those occasions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, I think at this moment, I have to remind you of the Rule 89(C) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which says, "A Trial Chamber may admit any relevant evidence which it deems to have probative value." So, so far as I understand it, there are only two criteria for the admission of the documents. One is the relevance. The other is the probative value. And it is the discretion of the Trial Chamber to make the decisions which means to see whether those documents are relevant or whether it has probative value. At this moment, I would like also to remind you a decision made by Appeals Chamber, which has the binding force on us. That is there is no legal basis that proof of the authenticity is a separate threshold requirement for the admissibility of documentary evidence. We believe that this Trial Chamber will act in accordance with the rules and with the decisions rendered by the Appeals Chamber. Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Before the witness comes back, can I just say something,? Mr. Krsnik you were so cross earlier that I was almost afraid to ask you if you were going to allow me any time to pose questions to -- what about the last witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We haven't finished with the last witness yet. Maybe just for another 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I had never known before doing this case that Croats were Latin people but I know now. What I wanted to know is I hope you won't be cross if I pose a few questions. I know your time is short and I promise I won't be long but because this man is from Siroki Brijeg, unless you have another witness from Siroki Brijeg, I'd like to ask him a few questions. Have you any other witness who is better qualified?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. There will be quite a number of them. And they are the witnesses who will be testifying -- I don't know whether we are in a private session but never mind, those who will be testifying about the Convicts Battalion and so on and so forth. As I promised I brought such witnesses. One of them will be a background witness but others will all be fact witnesses and we have a number of witnesses who were members and who will explain all the things about this Convicts Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Maybe I'll just pose a couple of questions. You're not to get cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You are very kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, witness, please sit down. We won't take a long time this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Witness, because you're of a certain age and you're a man of some authority in Siroki Brijeg, I wanted to ask you some questions that maybe I can't ask anybody else. Just for a start, how big is Siroki Brijeg? I'm sure I've been told but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the municipality of Siroki Brijeg.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Very good. The other question I wanted to ask you about was the Convicts Battalion. You explained to us its origin, that the founding members were people who had been persecuted in the past and who had either served prison sentences or had been forced to leave the country. And Mr. Naletilic was one of those people. When you talk about the persecution, can we take it safely that you're talking about persecution during the communist era?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: When did that era come to an end? When was it safe for people to express their views and maybe to return back to their native country?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could return when, in the eastern part of Europe, changes took place, and also when Yugoslavia fell apart, when it broke down to the former republics, and when -- and then they were free to return to their homeland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: So if you are saying that there was persecution and people were not allowed to express their political beliefs right up to 1989, would there be very young people, then, from Siroki Brijeg who would have been persecuted by the communist regime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, not only in Siroki Brijeg but also across the territory, it sufficed to start a song which the regime did not like, and you'd get at least three to six months of imprisonment. People, including young people under normal circumstances, did not naturally sing because they knew what that meant. But you have a drink or two and you are in a good mood, and on various special occasions, down there, all the Catholics and then at Christmas time or Easter time, people would naturally sing, and let's say even those prohibited songs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Are you saying, sir, that the prohibition on singing hymns was effective right up to 1989?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's say until 1989, perhaps a few years before that, in Croatia, for instance, in 1971, the spring, the so-called Croat Spring. And then there was some minor freedom which one could, in a -- that one could also practise even in our parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Rankovic was gone, who abdicated in 1966 and I can say that it was ever since then, since then, some small freedom set in which then finally arrived that year that you mentioned. Let me just mention a very simple song, Your Honours, if you're interested, and you will hear that you could earn a six month --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krsnik might get very cross because he has two witnesses who are anxious to given that evidence. So for that reason I have to ask you to try your best to be concise. Really what I want to know is would somebody as young as the late Mario Hrkac have been persecuted? Or served a prison sentence or been forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our area, we become of age at the age of 18, so whoever was 18 could be punished for anything, for a trifle little matter. So it was not just the persecution of young people but their fathers, who were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You missed my point. What I'm saying is somebody who was as young as the late Mr. Hrkac, relative to, say, Mr. Andabak or Mr. Naletilic, had he been persecuted, did he serve a prison sentence for his political views under the communist regime?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was enough to have family member who was an emigrant and you would be under the scrutiny of the then regime, the then police, and if Mario Hrkac -- I can't tell you anything concrete about him, but if he had had anybody in emigration, maybe you have read it somewhere, I think his uncle was liquidated by the UDBA, in Belgrade. So the entire Hrkac family was under scrutiny.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If I move on to something else, would you be able to assist us, and again you may not be able to because I know that you were not politically active prior to the war, what, as far as you understand, were the aims of the Convicts Battalion? I know you say that it was a group of people who had been persecuted, who started it, but what did they intend to do with the Convicts Battalion? Why did they start it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've tried to explain what the times were like, what was going on, and what was the risk, the danger, facing not only Siroki Brijeg but the entire area. So the general situation was far from being good. The Serbs had attacked. We experienced an unexpected shock, and we were under -- under the impression that the war -- there would never be another war in the former Yugoslavia. That's what they taught us as schools. And all of a sudden, we were attacked. People fled, they became refugees. And some people remained, stayed back in the territory, and we had to start organising ourselves to defend our homes, because these are our homes. These are Croatian homes. We don't want to flee Bosnia-Herzegovina. It is our homeland, in the same way it is the homeland of other peoples, and we wanted to live together with them. That's why we are never going to flee our homes. And we are going to fight as hard as we have to, to allow our children to grow in their homes, safely like any other child anywhere in the world. So that's why I'm trying to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I have to try and stop you, I'm sorry I don't want to be rude but I really need shorter questions and maybe you feel very deeply about this but we understand. What I want to know is do you know, and if you don't, say you don't, do you know what were the aims of the Convicts Battalion? Was it merely to be a defensive organisation in the attack which was coming from the Serbs? Or was it a special purpose, as you said, unit, for special tasks? I accept that anybody in a war wants to defend their homes, their families, et cetera, but were there any special motives in relation to the founding of the Convicts Battalion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only motive for the establishment of the Convicts Battalion was to preserve the area, to protect the area, to rally people around themselves. It was not easy. We were at the time very little people, and I can tell here, speaking in front of God, if there had been no -- that man over there, Mr. Naletilic, who had returned, and who tried to organise us to encourage us to tell us not to be afraid, to encourage us to stay where we were and try and protect our homes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You see, everything that you're saying is interesting but you've already told us before. I wanted specific answers to the questions and maybe you're not the right person to ask. Mr. Krsnik may have somebody else. One last question: Two last questions: Could anybody join the Convicts Battalion besides -- in other words, did they have to be associated with somebody who had been persecuted? Or could anybody able-bodied join?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody could join the Convicts Battalion whoever wanted to come to the defence of their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Thank you. That's presently. The next and my last question is at one stage yesterday you were telling us that there was a large number of detainees who needed to be housed somewhere, and that it was your job to find accommodation, and you had established where there would be 20 beds available. Where in the tobacco factory were these 20 beds located?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I still had the picture to show it to you, we are talking about a small number of detainees, so if we are talking about 20 of them, then I can show you exactly. It is in the Defence Department. There were a number of rooms which -- which had beds in them and that is where people could sleep. So six rooms for some 18 to 20 people. This is a long building and it had this part -- was separate from others. I can show it to you in the photo, if you'll allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: If the photograph is available conveniently but I think that building was pointed out to us by another witness. It has a sort of white roof, a long building towards the perimeter on the -- if it's convenient. If you could put the pointer on the location, once you've established where it is, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Behind this white building, behind this white building, there is a house which is almost as long as the front building itself. So in here, in one part are the Defence department premises and in its other part, there were detainees. And they had all the amenities, all the conditions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: You've been very helpful. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any questions out of Judge's question? Well, thank you very much, Witness, for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. We appreciate that very much. When the usher pulls down the blinds, you may go, and we all wish you a good journey home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours, through Witness NH, we would like to tender D1/344, due to the testimony of the witness, we'd ask that that be under seal. And.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. There is no --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: D1/345. And the picture, P26.9, as marked by the witness, is -- we gave it a number yesterday, Your Honour. D1/43.1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any objections? Mr. Scott? Since there is only three documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't believe so but I was just to be honest I was just pulling them back out again, if I could just look for a moment. No, Your Honour. There is no objections. There is no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. These three documents are admitted into evidence. Do you have any documents to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do. I would appreciate the Chamber's indulgence if I could again, especially in light of all the complaints that have been made in the last few days if I could go back through them and sort them to find which ones would actually be tendered, I would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may do that. Mr. Krsnik, could we have the next witness? And please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you. [The witness entered court].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry for keeping you waiting. You may sit -- I'm so sorry. Would you please make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I read it in my native language?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Whatever you like.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. First I would like to ask the technicians to lower the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness. In front of you is a monitor which helps us in communication, in order to make our interpreters lives easier. Please follow the cursor on the screen. I'm sure you won't find it a difficult, and we have to make sure that we don't overlap in our questions and answers. Now you're going to see a piece of paper with your name on it. Don't utter the name, just say, "Yes," if that is indeed your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Yes, this is my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to private session for a short while?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Can you continue, follow your -- the questions in front of you? You said there were several. So can you answer them one by one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Well, my relation to those detainees was -- I was asked by my brigade and municipality to talk to those guys and ask them if they were willing to join some action on digging certain channel or trench for power supply, to radio station repeater.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Who asked you to talk to them? And what was their answer? What was your duty in respect of these detainees? You had a certain task. What task did you have? Can you please tell that to the Honourable Court? I don't want to interrupt you all the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Well, since I was kind of a Home Guard and everybody knew that I Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 12073 to 12081. was a communicative person, they asked me to speak to those guys and ask them if they are willing to go out, because they were obviously bored, and to ask them if they were willing to help digging this trench. I was supposed -- and three other guys -- to prevent any kind of maltreating of those detainees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And they were whose responsibility? Who had brought them, if you know that, and why were they put up where they were put up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: I think that military police brought them in, and as they later told me when we started communicating, that they were suspected of certain crimes and were interrogated, and some of them were waiting the exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Will you now describe briefly, that was forced labour, and what kind of food did they -- were given, what kind of treatment they received? And then we shall go into private session to hear what others besides you were made responsible for them, who were there to take care of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Well, they were not forced to work. They were helping the workers, one other company from Siroki Brijeg, who were having the equipment and were doing the digging of the hard parts, and they were sort of removing the material, cutting the surrounding bushes and trees along the trench, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And what about the food? Where did you get your food from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Well, the food was common military food.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [no interpretation] Where was it prepared?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: It was cooked in a military kitchen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And where was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: That kitchen first was in the facilities of a company, Feal, F-E-A-L. And later on, in the facilities of Obnova company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were the detainees given some different food or did you all have the same kind of food? I mean prepared in that kitchen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: The food was same for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And when there were out on working sites, were they getting some better quality food or something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Well, it was sufficient and the leftovers were just taken back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge if they were also given cigarettes, or beer? Was that provided for? What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Yes. You could often see beers there. And cigarettes almost regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Were cigarettes also distributed amongst everybody? I mean the HVO soldiers? Was it the common practice to distribute them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: We almost regularly received cigarettes because nobody at that time had money enough, and it was the usual manner that the command would share cigarettes for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do they come as part of a -- relief or do you know what was the source, what was the provenance of those cigarettes, of course, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Very well. Will you please be so kind? I have a couple of questions and two photographs and that will be the end of it and I will hand you over to the Prosecutor. Tell me, please, did anyone mistreat them? Did somebody come to mistreat them? Did you see them receive blows or being bruised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: My co-counsel reminds me to ask you how did the work -- I mean how many hours did they work? When would they go out? When would they come back to their premises? What were the working hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Well, since this was during the summer time, when the weather is very hot, people usually work in this manner: You start your job, let's say 8.00 in the morning, then you work until approximately noon. Then you have lunch, beer and a short break. And then you wait for sun to set down a little bit. And let's say 4.00 in the afternoon, and then you work a bit more, let's say until about 8.00. And then we would go back downtown.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session just for a moment, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Now, from this spot to the house, was there any where that you took the detainees to, to carry out some work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: No, not at this spot. The works were done much closer to me, from my position. And down the slope on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Perhaps one can see it on photograph 26.2, where you went to perform those works. Take the pointer up, please, and let's take the tobacco station as your reference point. Will you point at that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: [indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. Can you see the building that you were housed in on this photograph? Where the detainees were put up? Can you please circle it and put "1".

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: [marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Are you aware if those other buildings at the tobacco station were in use in 1992 and 1993? Perhaps you can point to them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: No. The other facilities were out of usage. They were quite ruined and were not appropriate for use.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Okay. Very good. And will you please now try to see where this transmitter was and where is it that you performed the work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: It is not contained with this picture, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the right side, by this road, and then up the hill, and then to the right side, and I just can show it approximately like this, like here, somewhere like here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: But take the pointer to show us the last point. Can't see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... should go to the right and then up the hill. And a little bit backwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Right. Can we see at least the hill on this photograph? And will you then point at the last point of that hill, if that is you can find your way about this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: All right. The last one I believe we have another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, just one consultation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Could we have once again 26.1? Perhaps you'll be able to find your way about that photograph better, because my client tells me that one can see the transmitter. Perhaps you simply did not see it, did not get your bearings right on that photograph. 26.2?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This is an air photograph, so perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, just so we can get our bearings? Do you remember the first photograph that you showed this witness where he said from a point you couldn't see the house?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Could you relate that photograph, the area encompassed in that photograph on to this one, if it is in fact included? It's very unclear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Okay, because -- [Interpretation] Yes, this is an aerial photograph it's really not easy to discern that's why one can see the tobacco station very clearly all these buildings, right we've resolved that. Can we now have 25.2 back?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And perhaps you can show us here the last points and where is it that you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: From point 1 down to the left, and down the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope we were of some help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Do you see that stone building that looks like a grotto? That's what it looks like to me in the photographer, it's not clear. It's a sort of semicircular cut stone. It looks like the sort of thing that was fashionable in the 50s.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I haven't got my glasses on. I can't see that far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the middle of the photograph between the house and point 1? I see, look at it, does it look like a heap of stones?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know what that is, between point 1 and the house, you will see a hill, a mount of stones.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: You mean this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then the spot 1?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: It just shows how different it looks. That's clearly a tree, and on my photograph it looks like a stone-cut building. You just wonder what we are looking at. It would be very useful if we had this photograph because it's much clearer than what's on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Have you got enough photographs?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, from Madam Registrar. That's yours, that's your copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's your copy so we have to manage as best we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one final question to assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Look at the point marked by 1. What is -- what is that? This looks as if somebody was digging. Did you do that? What is that column or pylon? What is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: I don't know exactly what this pole is but I think that this is the beginning of the channel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: This pole or pylon, you don't know what it is, is that the electricity or what? Okay. Then, can we have the last photograph, please? Do you recognise what things you see in these photos? This is Exhibit D342.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Yeah, this is the building where the military police was situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And one final question, my colleague has reminded me to ask you: How long -- how much time did you spend with the detainees? You and the other four people you've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: With certain breaks, for about month and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Do you know whether they received any remuneration for the work that they did?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: I was told that the municipality authorities are going to give them certain amount of money. I don't know honestly how much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: And who did they give the money to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my client insists on us asking the Prosecution to give us the photo with the entire canal. Have you ever given that to us? From the transmission station to the end. Do we have that from you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I don't know, Your Honour, I don't know what they are talking about, some photograph that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because my client insists that that photo exists, that he has seen it here. I haven't seen it myself. The photo of that canal or channel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, maybe during the break we could look into the files to see whether there is a photo exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I understand it's time for the break. And we will have cross-examination after the break. We will resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there has been a misunderstanding between me and my client. My client claims that a photo was seen in this courtroom depicting the entire Cigansko Brdo. Allegedly that photo was taken from a helicopter and that photo depicts the canal with the transmission station, and I cannot seem to be able to convince him that even if it was in the courtroom, that it doesn't have to still be with Madam Registrar. He remembers the photo. We -- all of us Defence council have been discussing that issue and in that case, if that photo cannot be found, we all know that if it was exhibited in the courtroom, that it has to be in the files. That's what we are trying to tell our client, that there is no way that something can be shown once and then withdrawn. That it has to remain in the files. So he didn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think Judge Diarra is trying to say something that hasn't shown up in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DIARRA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said twice that your client should give us the number, the ID number, of that photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, during the break -- before the break, I asked Madam Registrar to look into the files to find that photo, if that is the case. But up to now, we have not received any positive report on that. I believe that Madam Registrar will keep looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, my colleague, Mr. Meek is looking at everything that has been shown in the courtroom. I hope that he will have a positive -- there will be a positive outcome, and if it cannot be found, then I shall ask to be able to bring back the witness for another time, because my client, I believe, is right, that since the witness is here, that he should be able to point exactly where things are, because what he was been shown has nothing to do with the house or around the house and I agree with my client on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, at this moment, we are not sure whether we could find this photo or not. So I think during the next hours, Madam Registrar will do her best and try to locate that photo. Could we --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Or, Your Honours, I can do something else. Maybe we can start the cross-examination because, realistically saying we cannot see the last witness, so let him stand until Monday, and over the weekend, maybe my client could tell me exactly what area he wants to see. Maybe I could organise that to be photographed over the weekend and sent here to the -- by the DHL, and then I would ask another question to this witness about that new photo, and then I would also allow cross-examination after that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the witness should remain under the oath, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we remember that a videotape was shown at that time that might indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was a videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Krsnik, I think we have to start the cross-examination of this witness right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And I'll give you the opportunity to bring up this matter again during your re-examination and I also believe that this subject will be subject to the cross-examination again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we have the witness, please? Any direct examination, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Cross-examination? Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The reference to taking the time when these Muslim children were evacuated from the hospital in East Mostar, just one or two questions on that. Do you have an approximate date, sir, of this event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: It was in the summer of 1993. June and July, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And was this a one-time -- a particular event that you say this Sally Baker wrote about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: There are two events regarding Mostar hospital, and one event regarding Nova Bila Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say in connection with the evacuation of the wounded and sick children from the hospital in East Mostar, on the east side, that's what I'm specifically directing your attention to at the moment. That happened on -- this evacuation happened on one occasion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: There were two evacuations from Mostar east.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And that was again during this June or July, 1993 time period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And on those occasions, were these efforts, these evacuation efforts, accompanied by, for instance, anyone from the Spanish Battalion or ECMM or any of the international agencies who were in the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Not on the very occasion of evacuation. Ms. Sally Baker, that I admire very much for her bravery, took our ambulance across the no-man's land into Mostar east, and we arranged sort of cease-fire for that occasions, but I was deeply concerned for her, for, you know, when you are going through the no-man's land, there always can be a soldier that is too nervous, or doesn't understand the situation, he just sees an ambulance coming in and he can shoot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. And my question is about this is not to it take anything away from the good effort that may have been made at that time. I just want to make sure that the Judges understand and I understand the event as closely as possible. So it was Ms. Baker who took an ambulance across into the east side, and it was not -- or did it include you and Mr. Bagaric or just Ms. Baker?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: She did it herself. She drove the ambulance across.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Then I take it then what happened is some Muslim children were brought back by Ms. Baker to the west side hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: Yes. And they were given the first aid, and we arranged all the papers for them to be transferred to Split hospital and further.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have a rough idea of how many children were involved in this occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
utterances.text: I imagine about ten.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall the nature of their wounds or the condition they were in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS NI
